title: Evidence base for model parameters
text:
This page summarizes the published evidence for every input in R/setup.R. It reports what the literature supports for each parameter and how strong that support is. It does not change the model: the values in setup.R are still the ones the website results use, and the table below compares them with the evidence.

Model version reviewed: commit f95f972 (19 Feb 2026). Parameter values were read from R/setup.R.
Setting: US deceased-donor kidney transplantation. Kidney-specific figures are not generalized to other organs.
Evidence cutoff: 19 Oct 2026. Searches covered PubMed (with PMC full text where available) and the web: journal sites, CDC, OPTN/SRTR, USRDS, BLS and BEA price indices, CMS fee schedules and drug-pricing sources.
Inclusion: donor-derived infection surveillance, diagnostic accuracy studies, transplant outcome cohorts, economic studies and price sources. Reviews were used to find primary studies and are not counted alongside them.
Access level: every figure is marked full text, abstract, or secondary (read through a summary, a news report or a copy of an official file). Abstract-only and secondary figures should be checked against the source before they are relied on.
Computed values: where a number was derived from reported counts (for example an exact binomial interval), it is marked computed. The source authors did not report it.
Verification: an independent re-read of the primary sources checked 17 key figures. 16 were confirmed. The 17th (Bowring 2018 hazard ratios) has no confidence intervals in the paper to check.
AI assistance: searching and extraction were done with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) and reviewed by the author. Items still to be checked by hand are listed in TODO.md.

Basis labels.

E: derived from evidence.
E+J: evidence-informed, with explicit judgment.
Elicit: no usable evidence; needs expert elicitation or new data. A broad prior is a placeholder until then.
Policy: a choice about practice, not an estimable quantity. Analyze as scenarios.

Ranges labeled scenario or judgment are not confidence intervals.

The three quantities that most affect the decision have no direct evidence:

how common CrAg positivity is among donors;
how often a screen-detected donor transmits infection;
what happens to a kidney from a CrAg-positive donor.

title: Evidence base for model parameters
text:
Donor and recipient epidemiology
The main US source is the OPTN Disease Transmission Advisory Committee (DTAC) report on donor-derived cryptococcosis, 2009–2019 (Penumarthi et al. 2021) (full text).









Parameter
Evidence
Supported range
Basis




p_usage
2024 kidney nonuse was 29.3% of recovered kidneys; 1.87 kidneys recovered and 1.32 transplanted per donor (OPTN/SRTR 2026; Lentine et al. 2026) (secondary). Nonuse is about 69% for KDPI ≥85% or donor age ≥65. Potential-to-actual donor conversion was 18.8% and 48.2% at two OPOs (Johnson et al. 2023) (abstract)
Kidney use given recovery 0.65–0.75 (about 0.3 for KDPI ≥85%)
E, once the unit is fixed


p_donor_cryptococcus
No donor screening study. Recognized US events, 2009–2019: 12 donors with proven or probable transmission, or 23 including donors whose recipients were protected by prophylaxis, among 101,006 deceased donors. That is 1.2–2.3 × 10⁻⁴ per donor (Penumarthi et al. 2021), a lower bound because recognition and reporting are incomplete
Scenario range 1 × 10⁻⁴ to 1 × 10⁻³
Elicit


p_transmission
Kidney recipients of transmitting donors: 13/19 infected (0.68; exact 95% CI 0.43–0.87, computed), 13/18 excluding the one recipient given prophylaxis. The 19 recipients came from 10 donors (Penumarthi et al. 2021, Table 1). All organs 23/34. All fungal pathogens in DTAC: 41/117 recipients (35%) (Kaul et al. 2016) (abstract). Single-cluster case reports (Baddley et al. 2011; Camargo et al. 2018; MacEwen et al. 2013) select on transmission and are not pooled
0.35–0.75 for clinically infected donors. No evidence for screen-detected, asymptomatic donors
E+J; Elicit


p_spont_cryptococcus
US kidney recipients 89/27,218 = 0.33% (exact CI 0.26–0.40%, computed) over about 3.5 years; median onset 616 days (George et al. 2017, Table 1). Taiwan 10.6 per 10,000 person-years (Chen et al. 2019) (abstract). Median onset 30.5 months in US Medicare kidney recipients (Fiorica et al. 2025)
0.002–0.01 cumulative over a stated multi-year horizon; about 0.001–0.002 per year
E



Why the transmission estimate is biased upward. A donor enters the DTAC series only if at least one recipient was infected and the infection was recognized. Those donors were also mostly ill: 10–11 of the 12 had CNS signs. Screening would mostly detect asymptomatic, low-titer donors, for whom no transmission data exist.
Clustering. Recipients of the same donor share the donor’s infection status. The 19 kidney recipients therefore carry much less information than 19 independent observations.
Prevalence versus reporting. Turning the recognized-event rate into a prevalence needs the share of infected donors whose recipients are recognized and reported. No study has measured it. A prevalence of 0.001 would mean only 12–23% of infected donors are ever recognized: plausible, but unsupported.
Overlapping cohorts. An IDWeek abstract on DTAC data for 2008–2017 (Mehta et al. 2018) overlaps the Penumarthi series and is not pooled with it.
Background infection timing. Most background cases occur long after any donor-directed antifungal course would end (median 616 days to 30.5 months). This matters for how prophylaxis efficacy is applied; see Management and prevention.
Structural notes.

Baseline kidney nonuse applies to both arms. Only incremental nonuse caused by a positive screen belongs to screening.
p_spont_cryptococcus needs the same horizon as the QALY and cost endpoints.

Sensitivity by disease spectrum.

Meningitis in HIV: about 99–100%.
Disseminated disease, HIV-negative: 82.6% (19/23) (Hevey et al. 2020).
Localized lung disease: 73–91% across studies.
Isolated lung disease in organ recipients: 73% (22/30) on older assays, including 0 of 4 lung recipients (Singh et al. 2008).

In the DTAC series, 11 of 12 transmitting donors had CNS signs, and 5 had a positive serum CrAg on retrospective testing (Penumarthi et al. 2021). No count of donors tested exists, so donor sensitivity cannot be computed.
What lowers specificity.

Defective IMMY lots. An FDA recall in December 2016 (US Food and Drug Administration 2016) and a field safety notice in January 2022 (IMMY Inc 2022) describe affected lots with about 90–91% specificity. Repeating the test on the same lot does not catch this.
Other assays. Dynamiker 66–86%; IMMY semi-quantitative 93.8–95.8%; Biosynex CryptoPS whole blood 96.6%, with a positive predictive value of 45.5%.
Cross-reactions. Trichosporon and related yeasts, and Aspergillus (2/29 false positives in one study).
Rheumatoid factor and hydroxyethyl starch. Shown for latex assays; no lateral-flow data. Relevant because donors may receive starch colloids.
No data on critically ill or brain-dead patients.

Confirmatory testing.

Acting only at titer ≥1:10 would remove most false positives, but in one study it kept only 39.6% of true positives among low-titer results.
Confirming with latex or EIA can wrongly discard true low-titer positives.
No study reports the joint accuracy of a two-step rule.
Errors on repeat testing are correlated (lot failures, specimen interference), so independence should not be assumed.

Supported ranges (judgment ranges, not fitted 95% intervals).

Sensitivity: center about 0.90–0.93; scenario range 0.75–0.99. The width reflects the unknown disease spectrum of screen-detected donors, not sampling error.
Specificity of one IMMY serum test without confirmation: center about 0.99–0.995; range 0.97–0.999.
Low-specificity scenario (about 0.90): a defective lot or a non-IMMY assay.
After confirmation: plausibly above 0.997, with an unquantified loss of sensitivity.

Biases in the accuracy studies. Most verified only positive results, some reference standards included the index test, and many compared cases with selected controls. A few counted true low-titer positives as false when the reference assay missed them.

title: Evidence base for model parameters
text:
Management and prevention
No published source supports the current values for cancellation (0.8), prophylaxis uptake (0.51) or prophylaxis efficacy (0.88), and the 2019 abstract gives none of them. Cancellation and uptake are better treated as policy or protocol scenarios than as estimated probabilities.
Guidelines. The AST guideline on donor-derived infections is Wolfe and Ison 2019 (Wolfe and Ison 2019). The AST cryptococcosis guideline is Baddley and Forrest 2019 (Baddley and Forrest 2019). Neither full text was retrievable, so their donor-specific recommendations are not summarized here. The 2024 global cryptococcosis guideline (Chang et al. 2024) makes no recommendation on donor screening.









Parameter
Evidence
Supported value or range
Basis




p_cancelled
No data on what happens to kidneys from known CrAg-positive donors. OPTN/DTAC guidance on donor CNS infection says organs from donors with diagnosed, treatable meningoencephalitis can be used if donor and recipients are treated (OPTN Ad Hoc Disease Transmission Advisory Committee 2012). No guideline found recommends discarding kidneys from a CrAg-positive donor. Closest proxy: a PHS increased-risk label raised kidney discard 1.13–2.17-fold by donor quality (Bowring et al. 2018) (full text), and was associated with discard at OR 1.20 (1.15–1.29) (Ariyamuthu et al. 2020) (abstract)
Scenarios 0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0; split true versus false positive and decline-and-reallocate versus discard
Policy


p_prophrate
Only observed rate: DTAC donors whose recipients were protected by prophylaxis, 20/35 recipients (57%) given it. The abstract says 23/35; the Results support 20 (Penumarthi et al. 2021)
Status quo 0.41–0.72 (about 0.34–0.78 allowing for clustering within donors). Protocol scenarios 0.8–1.0
E+J; Policy


p_prophefficacy
No comparative data in exposed transplant recipients. DTAC counts (disease in 4/7 recipients given any antifungal versus 19/27 not) are confounded and cannot be read as efficacy. Cochrane review of HIV primary prophylaxis: cryptococcal disease RR 0.29 (0.17–0.49), 7 RCTs, n≈5,000, an RRR of 0.71 (0.51–0.83) (Awotiwon et al. 2018) (full text). CrAg-negative trial: 1/760 versus 18/759 (Parkes-Ratanshi et al. 2011) (abstract; included in the Cochrane pool). Pre-emptive fluconazole in CrAg-positive HIV patients: meningitis 5.7% (3.0–9.7) treated versus 21.4% (11.6–34.4) untreated, across studies (Temfack et al. 2019) (abstract). 3/21 treated patients developed meningitis (Meya et al. 2010)
Donor-derived risk: center about 0.7; scenario range 0.3–0.95 (judgment)
E+J; Elicit



Efficacy against background infection. Background cryptococcosis in kidney recipients occurs at a median of about 20–30 months, long after any donor-directed course ends. A transparent alternative to applying full efficacy is efficacy multiplied by the share of the background-risk window the course covers: a judgment of about 0.05–0.25, or 0 in the base case.
Titer. About a third of asymptomatic CrAg-positive HIV patients already had meningitis, predicted by a blood titer above 1:160 (Wake et al. 2018) (abstract). Transmission and prophylaxis efficacy may both depend on donor titer.
Regimen and interactions.

No verified pre-emptive regimen for transplant recipients was found. The global guideline gives HIV regimens only (Chang et al. 2024).
Kidney case reports treat established disease with fluconazole 300–400 mg/day for 9–24 months, an upper bound for prophylaxis.
Tacrolimus needs about a 20% dose reduction with low-dose fluconazole (Johnston et al. 2022) or about one-third with treatment doses (Cheng et al. 2022) (both abstract), with close level monitoring.
No quantified estimate of fluconazole harm in kidney recipients was found.

Health outcomes
The current 5.5-QALY gain is plausible only against a dialysis-forever reference.

Against decline-and-wait, US models that allow later transplantation put the per-offer gain from accepting a good kidney at roughly 0.1–1.2 QALYs, usually with a cost saving.
No source estimates the penalty for declining after a positive CrAg screen. Every accept-versus-decline figure comes from another decline reason (high KDPI, an infectious-risk label, HCV viremia, older DCD donors), so applying them here is a judgment.

Transplant versus dialysis forever
Axelrod et al. (Axelrod et al. 2018) (full text, Table 3) is the best US source: 10-year horizon, 3% discounting, 2016 USD. Dialysis yields 4.03 QALYs.

KDPI ≤85: 6.07 QALYs, +2.04 and +$169 versus dialysis.
KDPI >85: +1.17 QALYs and +$38,459.
PHS increased-risk donor: +1.88 QALYs and +$14,935.

Its percentiles describe variation between simulated patients, not parameter uncertainty. No full-text lifetime US estimate confirming or refuting 5.5 QALYs was found.
Utilities. Transplant 0.82 (0.74–0.90) and dialysis 0.70 (0.62–0.78) (Wyld et al. 2012, Table 2). Sample their difference, −0.11 (−0.15 to −0.08), rather than the two independently.


Loss from recipient cryptococcosis
No utility weight or QALY decrement for cryptococcosis after transplant has been published. q_loss_cryptococcus has to be built from excess mortality, graft loss with return to dialysis, an acute decrement during treatment and any lasting neurological deficit.

Abstract



Lasting neurological deficits are documented only outside transplantation: residual visual impairment in 54% of HIV-negative survivors in Vietnam (Chau et al. 2010), and moderate-to-severe cognitive impairment in 63% of HIV patients in Uganda at 12 weeks (Nsangi et al. 2025).


Dependencies to respect in the model

Shared drivers. ICU admission, AKI and renal failure drive both cryptococcosis mortality and hospital cost, so disease cost and QALY loss should rise together. No source gives a correlation coefficient.
One wait-time input. The accept-now QALY gain and its cost saving both grow with the expected extra wait and shrink as KDPI rises. Model them as joint functions of one wait-time input, not as independent draws.
Same endpoint. q_loss_cryptococcus must be measured against the same accept-now endpoint it is subtracted from. If an early death makes the loss exceed the accept-now gain, the cryptococcosis endpoint falls below decline-and-wait; that is plausible and should not be truncated.
Not confidence intervals. Differences between Ellison’s candidate profiles are recipient heterogeneity, and microsimulation intervals such as Yanev’s (Yanev et al. 2021) are Monte Carlo error.

section: How much to trust these numbers
text:
How much to trust these numbers
The base case uses single best estimates, several of which have weak evidence behind them (see the evidence review). Two structural assumptions matter most for this result:

A cancelled transplant is treated as no transplant at all. If the intended recipient is usually transplanted later from another donor, the QALY loss from each false positive is much smaller than the model assumes. See known limitations.
A few inputs drive the result. In the one-way sensitivity analysis, the inputs that move net monetary benefit the most are p_specificity, q_nocryptococcus, p_usage. The scenario analyses show what happens if positive screens rarely lead to cancellation.

title: How the inputs are chosen
text: The decision model needs a value for every probability, cost and QALY on the tree. This page explains, in plain terms, how each input is given two things: a best estimate, used for the base case, and a range of plausible values, used in the sensitivity analyses. The full list of inputs, with their values and ranges, is on the Setup and parameters page.

title: How the inputs are chosen
section: Best estimates and where they come from
text:
Best estimates and where they come from
Each input’s best estimate is its base-case value, stored in R/setup.R. The evidence review sets out the published evidence for every input, grades how strong that evidence is, and labels each input by its basis: derived from evidence, evidence combined with judgment, needing expert elicitation because no usable evidence exists, or a policy choice best analyzed as a scenario. The review does not change the model. The values used throughout this site are still those in R/setup.R, and the review notes where the evidence points to different values.

title: How the inputs are chosen
text:
Describing uncertainty with probability distributions
A single best estimate hides how uncertain it is. A donor CrAg positivity of 1 in 1,000 might be known to within a few percent, or might be off by a factor of three. To capture this, each uncertain input is given a prior distribution: a curve that says which values are plausible and how plausible each is. The probabilistic sensitivity analysis draws values from these curves, and the one-way sensitivity analysis uses their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the low and high values.
Two families of curves are used, chosen to respect what each kind of input can be.
Probabilities use Beta distributions, which can only take values between 0 and 1. A useful way to read a Beta distribution with parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is as the result of an imaginary study with about \(\alpha\) events among \(\alpha + \beta\) patients. In this model every probability has \(\alpha\) = 10, and \(\beta\) is then set so that the mean equals the base-case value. Every probability is therefore described as roughly as certain as a study that observed 10 events. For example:

Transmission from an infected donor (p_transmission, base case 0.867) has a 95% range of 0.63 to 0.99.
Donor CrAg positivity (p_donor_cryptococcus, base case 0.001) is described as roughly as certain as finding 10 infected donors among 10,000 screened, and has a 95% range of 0.00048 to 0.0017.

Costs and QALYs use gamma distributions, which cannot be negative and have a long right tail: most values sit near the mean, but occasional values are much larger. This suits costs in particular, where a few complicated hospital stays cost far more than a typical one. In this model every gamma distribution has shape \(k\) = 4, so its standard deviation is 50% of its mean and its 95% range runs from about 0.27 to 2.2 times the base-case value. For example, the cost of an episode of cryptococcosis (cost_disease, base case $110,945) ranges from about $30,200 to $243,000.
Using the same \(\alpha\) for every probability and the same \(k\) for every cost and QALY is a simplification: the width of each range follows from these shared settings, not from the strength of the evidence behind each input. For costs and QALYs it gives every input the same relative spread. For probabilities it treats each as if about 10 events had been observed, which gives rare probabilities, such as donor CrAg positivity, a much wider range relative to their value than common ones, such as test specificity. The evidence review compares these ranges with what the literature supports for each input.

Inputs that are not varied
Some inputs are fixed at their base-case value in every analysis: cost_cancellation, cost_nocryptococcus, cost_nonacceptance, q_noacceptance. These are the costs and QALYs of outcomes measured against the reference point of no transplant with continued dialysis. number_donors is also not varied; it is a label and does not enter the calculation.


Inputs are varied independently
In the probabilistic sensitivity analysis each input is drawn separately, as if the inputs were unrelated. Some are probably related in reality. A more severe episode of cryptococcosis, for example, is likely both to cost more and to cause a larger QALY loss. Drawing related inputs independently can make the spread of results narrower or wider than it should be. Independent draws can also produce combinations that are clinically implausible: because q_nocryptococcus and q_loss_cryptococcus are drawn separately, about one draw in seven gives a QALY loss from cryptococcosis larger than the QALY gain from the transplant itself.

text:
Parameters of the model

Probabilities
We parameterize the probability portion of the model based on the beta distribution.
The beta distribution is a way of representing uncertainty around a probability—that is, a number that must fall between 0 and 1, such as a risk, sensitivity, specificity, or event rate.
For a beta distribution with parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), the mean is given by \(\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)\). The confidence interval associated with these parameters can also be derived from these parameters.
We chose values of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) which yield the mean from the base case analysis and confidence intervals consistent with prior literature.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
text: This page explains the ideas behind a cost-effectiveness analysis for readers who have not worked with one before. It is written for transplant and infectious diseases clinicians. Nothing here is specific to cryptococcus: the next pages describe the decision model, how its inputs are chosen and how uncertainty is analyzed.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
section: The question a cost-effectiveness analysis asks
text:
The question a cost-effectiveness analysis asks
Clinical studies usually ask whether one strategy produces better health than another. A cost-effectiveness analysis asks a second question: is the extra health worth what it costs? It does not ask which strategy is cheapest. A strategy that costs more can be the better use of resources if the health it buys is large enough, and a strategy that saves money can be a poor choice if the health it gives up is too valuable.
The analysis on this site compares two strategies for deceased kidney donors:

No screening, the current standard approach (see Clinical background), and
Screening every donor with a serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test, with the downstream decisions a positive result triggers.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
text:
Thinking incrementally
Every result on this site is incremental: it is the difference between screening and no screening, not the total for either strategy alone. Two numbers summarize that difference:

ΔC, the incremental cost: the expected cost with screening minus the expected cost without it. A negative ΔC means screening saves money.
ΔQ, the incremental health effect: the expected quality-adjusted life years (QALYs, explained below) with screening minus those without it. A negative ΔQ means screening, on average, costs health.

Both numbers are expected values: averages over everything that could happen to a donor and the recipient, each outcome weighted by how likely it is. A screening program that occasionally prevents a devastating infection, but more often leads to a usable kidney being declined after a false-positive result, can come out ahead or behind on average. The expected value is how a decision model weighs the rare catastrophe against the common, smaller harm.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
section: Measuring health: the quality-adjusted life year
text:
Measuring health: the quality-adjusted life year
Transplant outcomes are not only about survival. A year with a functioning graft and a year on dialysis are both a year alive, but they are not equivalent to patients. The quality-adjusted life year (QALY) captures both length and quality of life in one number (Whitehead and Ali 2010):
\[
\text{QALYs} = \text{years lived} \times \text{utility}
\]
A utility is a weight, usually between 0 (a state as bad as death) and 1 (full health); states judged worse than death can score below 0. Utilities come from patients or members of the public valuing health states with standardized methods. In a meta-analysis of kidney disease treatments, the pooled utility was about 0.82 for a functioning kidney transplant and about 0.70 for dialysis (Wyld et al. 2012). Ignoring discounting (described below), ten years with a functioning graft is therefore worth about 8.2 QALYs, and ten years on dialysis about 7.0 QALYs. That difference of about 1.2 QALYs holds survival equal and reflects quality of life alone. In practice a transplant also lengthens survival compared with dialysis, so the real difference is larger.
For a donor-screening question this matters in two directions. Preventing a case of donor-derived cryptococcosis protects QALYs, because the disease causes deaths, graft losses and long hospitalizations. Declining a kidney that would have functioned well loses QALYs, because the intended recipient stays on dialysis longer. The QALY lets the model put both on the same scale.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
text:
Putting cost and health together

The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
The traditional summary is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER):
\[
\text{ICER} = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta Q}
\]
the extra cost per extra QALY gained. An ICER of $40,000 per QALY means screening buys each additional QALY for $40,000.
The ratio is easy to misread when ΔQ is close to zero or negative. An ICER of −$40,000 per QALY could mean screening saves money and improves health, or that it costs money and harms health: the sign alone does not say which. A ratio also becomes unstable as its denominator approaches zero, which is common when the health difference between strategies is small, as it is when both cryptococcosis and false-positive screens are rare.


Net monetary benefit
For these reasons this site reports net monetary benefit (NMB) instead, the dollar form of the net benefit framework (Stinnett and Mullahy 1998):
\[
\text{NMB} = \text{WTP} \times \Delta Q - \Delta C
\]
WTP is the willingness-to-pay threshold: the most a health system is prepared to spend to gain one QALY. NMB converts the health difference into dollars at that rate and subtracts the extra cost. The rule is simple:

NMB greater than zero: screening is cost-effective at that threshold.
NMB less than zero: it is not.

A worked example: suppose screening gains 0.01 QALYs per donor (ΔQ = +0.01) and adds $500 per donor (ΔC = +$500). At $100,000 per QALY, NMB = $100,000 × 0.01 − $500 = +$500, so screening would be cost-effective. If instead it lost 0.01 QALYs and saved $500, NMB = −$1,000 + $500 = −$500: the money saved would not make up for the health given up.
NMB and the ICER always agree about the decision when ΔQ is positive: screening is cost-effective when the ICER is below the threshold. When ΔQ is negative the rule reverses, and screening is cost-effective only when the ICER is above the threshold, meaning each QALY given up saves more than the threshold. NMB needs no such reversal. It also averages cleanly: the mean NMB across many simulations equals the NMB of the mean costs and QALYs, which is not true of a mean of ratios. This matters for the probabilistic sensitivity analysis.


Choosing a willingness-to-pay threshold
There is no official or consensus US threshold (Vanness et al. 2021). A figure of $50,000 per QALY was long quoted, but its origins are obscure and it has not kept pace with inflation; Neumann and colleagues argued that $100,000 to $150,000 per QALY is more defensible (Neumann et al. 2014). One estimate, based on the health lost when higher spending raises insurance premiums and people drop coverage, put the threshold at about $104,000 per QALY in 2019 dollars (95% uncertainty interval $51,000 to $209,000) (Vanness et al. 2021). This analysis uses $100,000 per QALY, and the acceptability curve shows how the conclusion changes across thresholds from $0 to $200,000.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
text:
The cost-effectiveness plane
The cost-effectiveness plane plots ΔQ on the horizontal axis and ΔC on the vertical axis, so each strategy compared with its alternative is a point (Black 1990). The four quadrants have different meanings:








Figure 1: The four quadrants of the cost-effectiveness plane. The dashed line is the willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000 per QALY. Points in the shaded region, below and to the right of the line, are cost-effective.






Lower right, cheaper and more effective: screening dominates. It should be adopted whatever the threshold.
Upper left, more costly and less effective: screening is dominated. It should not be adopted.
Upper right, more costly and more effective: a trade-off. Screening is cost-effective if each QALY gained costs less than the threshold, which is the region below the dashed line.
Lower left, cheaper and less effective: also a trade-off, and the one clinicians find least intuitive. Screening saves money but costs health. It is cost-effective only if the savings are large enough: more than the threshold for every QALY lost, which again is the region below the dashed line.

The dashed line marks NMB = 0. Points below and to the right of it have positive NMB; points above and to the left have negative NMB. A strategy that saves money but loses health falls in the lower-left quadrant, and whether it is acceptable depends entirely on how much money is saved per QALY lost.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
text:
Perspective, time horizon and discounting
Three choices shape any cost-effectiveness analysis. The US Second Panel on Cost-Effectiveness in Health and Medicine set out recommended practice for each (Sanders et al. 2016), and the CHEERS 2022 statement lists what a report should state about them (Husereau et al. 2022).

Perspective: whose costs count. A health care sector perspective counts medical costs, whoever pays them. A societal perspective adds costs outside health care, such as time away from work and caregiving. The Second Panel recommends reporting both.
Time horizon: how long the consequences are followed. The horizon should be long enough to capture every important difference between the strategies (Sanders et al. 2016). For a kidney transplant decision that can mean the life of the graft or the recipient.
Discounting: how future costs and QALYs are weighted. Costs and health that arrive in the future are given less weight than those that arrive now. The Second Panel recommends discounting both costs and QALYs at 3% a year.

The decision model page states how the current version of this model handles each of these.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
section: What a cost-effectiveness analysis does not tell you
text:
What a cost-effectiveness analysis does not tell you

It is about averages. The results describe the expected outcome across many donors and recipients. They do not predict what will happen with a particular donor, and they do not replace clinical judgment about a specific organ offer.
It depends on its inputs. Many of the inputs for donor cryptococcal screening are uncertain, and some have no direct evidence at all. The evidence review grades the support for each input, and the sensitivity analyses show which uncertainties change the conclusion.
It values all QALYs equally. A QALY gained by a recipient who would otherwise wait years on dialysis counts the same as one gained by a recipient with many other options; the QALY approach does not weigh fairness or priority (Whitehead and Ali 2010). Other consequences of a donor-derived infection, such as its effect on trust in the transplant system, also sit outside the calculation.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis for clinicians
text:
Further reading
The Second Panel’s recommendations (Sanders et al. 2016) and the CHEERS 2022 reporting checklist (Husereau et al. 2022) are the standard references for US cost-effectiveness analysis. Briggs and colleagues describe how uncertainty in model inputs should be analyzed and reported (Briggs et al. 2012).

title: Clinical background
text:
Cryptococcosis in kidney transplant recipients is uncommon but potentially catastrophic. When transmission occurs through the donor, it often presents early after transplant, may involve the central nervous system, and is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality despite treatment.
Because donor-derived cryptococcosis is rare, organ procurement organizations do not routinely screen donors for cryptococcus. Instead, current practice typically relies on:

clinical donor history,
cause of death,
gross or histopathologic findings, and
post-transplant vigilance.

However, advances in antigen testing and increasing attention to donor-derived infections have renewed debate about whether systematic donor screening could prevent severe outcomes at an acceptable cost.

title: Clinical background
text:
Why screening is controversial
Routine cryptococcal screening of donors raises several competing concerns:

Low incidence: Donor-derived cryptococcosis is rare, so most screened donors would test negative.
False positives: Even highly specific tests can generate false positives when prevalence is very low, potentially leading to unnecessary organ discard or recipient prophylaxis.
Downstream consequences: A positive donor test may trigger recipient antifungal treatment, delayed transplant, or organ non-use, each with its own harms and costs.
Severe consequences when missed: When donor-derived infection does occur, outcomes can be devastating.

Because these tradeoffs involve rare events with high impact, intuition alone is often insufficient to guide policy.

What this analysis does
This project uses decision-analytic modeling to evaluate different strategies for managing cryptococcus risk in organ donors. In practical terms, the analysis asks:

If we adopt a particular donor screening or management strategy, what are the expected clinical outcomes and costs across many transplants?

    "Screening","Accept","Positive","CrAg+","Not Cancelled","Fluconazole","No cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_cryptococcus*p_sensitivity*p_nocancelled*p_prophrate*p_nobreakthrough_donorpos,cost_test+cost_nocryptococcus+cost_fluconazole,q_nocryptococcus,
    "Screening","Accept","Positive","CrAg+","Not Cancelled","None","Recipient cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_cryptococcus*p_sensitivity*p_nocancelled*p_noprophrate*p_transmission,cost_test+cost_disease,q_cryptococcus,
    "Screening","Accept","Positive","CrAg+","Not Cancelled","None","No cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_cryptococcus*p_sensitivity*p_nocancelled*p_noprophrate*p_nontransmission,cost_test+cost_nocryptococcus,q_nocryptococcus,

    "Screening","Accept","Negative","CrAg+","Not Cancelled","None","No cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_nocryptococcus*p_falsepositive*p_nocancelled*p_noprophrate*p_nospont_cryptococcus,cost_test+cost_nocryptococcus,q_nocryptococcus,
    "Screening","Accept","Negative","CrAg-",NA,NA,"Recipient cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_nocryptococcus*p_specificity*p_spont_cryptococcus,cost_test+cost_disease,q_cryptococcus,
    "Screening","Accept","Negative","CrAg-",NA,NA,"No cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_nocryptococcus*p_specificity*p_nospont_cryptococcus,cost_test+cost_nocryptococcus,q_nocryptococcus,
    "Screening","Non-accept",NA,NA,NA,NA,"Non-accept",p_nonusage,cost_nonacceptance+cost_test,q_noacceptance,
    
  )%>%
    mutate(cost_expected=probability*cost_total,
           qaly_expected=probability*qaly_total)
  
  #Summary object is created via summarize and then converted into long format
  summary_tibble<-path_table%>%

    summarize(total_expected_cost=sum(cost_expected), total_expected_qaly=sum(qaly_expected))%>%

      values_from = c(
        total_expected_cost,
        total_expected_qaly
      ),
      names_sep = "_"
    )
  
  #Final return
  return(summary_tibble)
}

Running and drawing the tree for one set of parameters
create_tree_diagram_QC() takes the same parameters as calculate_cost_QALY_QC(), with base-case defaults. It returns a list containing the pathway table, a summary by strategy, a table of the input parameters, the incremental cost, QALYs and net monetary benefit of screening, and the tree drawn by plot_tree_diagram_QC(). The base-case and scenario analyses use this function.

#Function that creates tree diagram.  It returns the diagram created via the GraphViz language, a table of input parameters
#and the output results from running the CEA on the parameterized decision tree.
#Default parameters for the decision tree are those of the base case as determined by the values of the expected_value
#list defined in the setup.R file
create_tree_diagram_QC<-function(p_usage=expected_value$p_usage, 
                                 p_donor_cryptococcus=expected_value$p_donor_cryptococcus, 
                                 p_transmission=expected_value$p_transmission, 
                                 p_spont_cryptococcus=expected_value$p_spont_cryptococcus, 
                                 p_sensitivity=expected_value$p_sensitivity,
                                 p_specificity=expected_value$p_specificity, 
                                 p_cancelled=expected_value$p_cancelled, 
                                 p_prophrate=expected_value$p_prophrate, 
                                 p_prophefficacy=expected_value$p_prophefficacy,
                                 number_donors=expected_value$number_donors,
                                 cost_test=expected_value$cost_test,
                                 cost_disease=expected_value$cost_disease,
                                 cost_fluconazole=expected_value$cost_fluconazole,
                                 cost_cancellation=expected_value$cost_cancellation,
                                 cost_nocryptococcus=expected_value$cost_nocryptococcus,
                                 cost_nonacceptance=expected_value$cost_nonacceptance,
                                 q_nocryptococcus=expected_value$q_nocryptococcus,
                                 q_noacceptance=expected_value$q_noacceptance,
                                 q_loss_cryptococcus=expected_value$q_loss_cryptococcus,
                                 circle_diameter=1.4,
                                 box_width=1.7,
                                 box_height=1,
                                 diamond_width=3,
                                 diamond_height=1.5
                                 
)
{
  
  #Define parameters that are derived from parameters passed to the function
  p_nonusage<-1-p_usage
  p_donor_nocryptococcus<-1-p_donor_cryptococcus
  p_nontransmission<-1-p_transmission
  p_nospont_cryptococcus<-1-p_spont_cryptococcus
  p_falsenegative<-1-p_sensitivity
  p_falsepositive<-1-p_specificity
  p_nocancelled<-1-p_cancelled
  p_noprophrate<-1-p_prophrate
  p_noprophefficacy<-1-p_prophefficacy
  p_breakthrough_donorpos<-(1-p_prophefficacy)*p_transmission
  p_nobreakthrough_donorpos<-1-p_breakthrough_donorpos
  p_breakthrough_donorneg<-(1-p_prophefficacy)*p_spont_cryptococcus
  p_nobreakthrough_donorneg<-1-p_breakthrough_donorneg
  q_cryptococcus<-q_nocryptococcus-q_loss_cryptococcus
  
  
  #Define return list
  return_list<-list()
  
  #Define tibble of outcomes
  return_list$path_table<-tribble(
    ~strategy, ~acceptance, ~donor_dz_status, ~donor_test_result, ~cancellation, ~proph, ~outcome, ~probability, ~cost_total, ~qaly_total,
    "No Screening","Accept","Positive",NA,NA,NA,"Recipient cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_cryptococcus*p_transmission,cost_disease,q_cryptococcus,
    "No Screening","Accept","Positive",NA,NA,NA,"No cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_cryptococcus*p_nontransmission,cost_nocryptococcus,q_nocryptococcus,
    "No Screening","Accept","Negative",NA,NA,NA,"Recipient cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_nocryptococcus*p_spont_cryptococcus,cost_disease,q_cryptococcus,
    "No Screening","Accept","Negative",NA,NA,NA,"No cryptococcus",p_usage*p_donor_nocryptococcus*p_nospont_cryptococcus,cost_nocryptococcus,q_nocryptococcus,

title: The decision model
text:
NoteModel version



This page describes the model as implemented in R/functions.R and R/setup.R in October 2026. Several structural choices are under review, and are listed under Known limitations. The numbers quoted on this page are read from R/setup.R when the page is rendered.
If you have not worked with cost-effectiveness analysis before, the primer explains the terms used here.

title: The decision model
text:
What is a decision tree?
A decision tree is a structured “if-this-then-that” map that compares two strategies (in this case, screen donors vs don’t screen) by averaging what would happen across many similar donors/recipients, weighting each possible outcome by its probability, and then adding up the costs and QALYs along the way.

title: The decision model
text:
Conceptual decision tree
First, we sketch out a decision tree that reflects our conceptual understanding of how costs and QALYs are generated by the two strategies. Note: Click to enlarge the diagram below:

At the far left, we have a decision node (square) splitting into the two strategies:

Screening (e.g., CrAg or other donor testing strategy)
No screening (standard approach)

After you pick a strategy, you hit chance nodes (circles). Each branch represents an outcome that can happen, like:

Donor truly has cryptococcal infection (rare)
Test is positive or negative (if screening)
Transmission occurs vs does not occur
Recipient develops disease vs not
Prophylaxis given or not, and whether it prevents disease

At the end of each pathway (a “leaf” of the tree), we assign values to terminal nodes:

Cost: testing costs, prophylaxis, hospitalization, antifungals, ICU care, etc.
QALYs: quality-adjusted survival for the recipient under that outcome

We assume that no transplant and the continuation of dialysis is the reference, such that ΔCost and ΔQALY are defined to be 0 and all other costs and QALYs are relative to this reference.

title: The decision model
text:
Walking through the tree
The sections below follow the tree from left to right, as a donor and the intended recipient would move through it. The probability on each branch is a model input; the probability of the branch beside it is always 1 minus that input, so the branches leaving every chance node add up to 1.

Step 1: are the kidneys used?
Each pathway starts with one potential donor. With probability p_usage (base case 0.43), the donor’s kidneys are used for transplant; otherwise they are not used, for reasons unrelated to cryptococcus. This first branch is the same in both strategies, so screening is not blamed for organ non-use that would have happened anyway.

Kidneys not used: cost cost_nonacceptance ($0) and QALYs q_noacceptance (0). This is the reference outcome: the intended recipient stays on dialysis, and its value is set to zero by definition rather than estimated.
In the screening strategy, the donor is tested whether or not the kidneys are used, so the test cost cost_test ($2) is added to every screening pathway, including this one.



Step 2: does the donor have cryptococcal infection?
With probability p_donor_cryptococcus (base case 0.001), a donor whose kidneys are used has cryptococcal infection that a serum CrAg test could detect. The evidence review discusses why this value is uncertain: no study has screened US deceased donors systematically.


Step 3a: no screening
Without screening, nobody knows the donor’s status, so every kidney is transplanted without prophylaxis.

Note: a recipient of a kidney from an infected donor faces only the transmission risk. If transmission does not occur, the model gives that recipient no background risk, so the two risks are not added together.


Step 3b: screening
With screening, the donor’s CrAg result comes back before the transplant decision.
The test. An infected donor tests positive with probability p_sensitivity (base case 0.901). An uninfected donor tests negative with probability p_specificity (base case 0.98), so 1 − p_specificity of uninfected donors test falsely positive.
After a negative test, the transplant goes ahead with no prophylaxis. An infected donor with a false-negative result transmits infection with probability p_transmission, exactly as without screening. An uninfected donor’s recipient faces the background risk p_spont_cryptococcus.
After a positive test, two decisions follow, and the model treats true and false positives the same way at each one because, at the time, the transplant team cannot tell them apart:

Cancel the transplant? With probability p_cancelled (base case 0.8), the transplant is cancelled. The recipient gets the reference outcome (no transplant, dialysis continues), and the costs are cost_cancellation ($0) plus the test.
If the transplant proceeds, give fluconazole prophylaxis? With probability p_prophrate (base case 0.51), the recipient receives prophylaxis at cost cost_fluconazole ($6,660). Prophylaxis reduces the risk of disease by the fraction p_prophefficacy (base case 0.88):

for a truly infected donor, the risk falls from p_transmission to (1 − p_prophefficacy) × p_transmission;
for a falsely positive donor, the risk falls from p_spont_cryptococcus to (1 − p_prophefficacy) × p_spont_cryptococcus.

Without prophylaxis, the risks are the same as without screening.



Step 4: the ends of the pathways
Every pathway ends in one of three outcomes. Costs and QALYs are measured relative to the reference outcome of no transplant with continued dialysis, which is why that outcome is worth zero of each.

In the screening strategy the test cost (cost_test) is added to every pathway, including those where the kidneys are not used. When fluconazole is given, cost_fluconazole is added whether or not the recipient later develops cryptococcosis; the regimen and its duration are not specified in the model.
Read in clinical terms:

q_nocryptococcus is the QALY gain from receiving this transplant rather than staying on dialysis.
q_loss_cryptococcus is the part of that gain lost when the recipient develops cryptococcosis, through death, graft loss or prolonged illness.
cost_nocryptococcus is meant to be the difference in cost between a transplant and staying on dialysis. Its current value, −$10, is a placeholder close to zero, not an estimate of that difference.
cost_disease is the cost of an episode of cryptococcosis in a transplant recipient. On the cryptococcosis pathway it replaces cost_nocryptococcus rather than being added to it.

One consequence is easy to miss. A cancelled transplant avoids the cost and the risk of cryptococcosis as well as the benefit of the transplant. Cancelling after a positive screen therefore lowers the expected cost of the screening strategy, while losing the full QALY gain of the transplant. The base case results show how much each of these contributes.

title: The decision model
text:
From pathways to results
For each strategy, the model multiplies each pathway’s probability by its cost and by its QALYs, and adds them up. This gives the expected cost and expected QALYs per potential donor for that strategy. The results pages report the differences between the strategies:

ΔC = expected cost with screening − expected cost without screening
ΔQ = expected QALYs with screening − expected QALYs without screening
NMB = 100,000 × ΔQ − ΔC, using the willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000 per QALY set in R/setup.R

The same calculation is run once for the base case, once per scenario in the scenario analyses, three times per input in the one-way sensitivity analysis (at the 2.5th percentile, the base-case value and the 97.5th percentile of the input’s distribution, described on How the inputs are chosen), and 10,000 times in the probabilistic sensitivity analysis. The code is on the Functions page.

title: The decision model
text:
The unit of analysis
All results are per potential donor entering the tree: one donor, whose kidneys may or may not be used, and one intended recipient. They are expected values, so a result such as “−0.04 QALYs” is an average across many donors, almost all of whom are uninfected and test negative.
The tree diagram labels its starting node with number_donors (702). That number is a label carried over from the original conference abstract. The model does not multiply by it, so the results are per donor, not totals for 702 donors.

title: The decision model
section: How this model handles perspective, time horizon and discounting
text:
How this model handles perspective, time horizon and discounting
The primer explains why these choices matter. In the current version of the model:

Perspective. The model counts only medical costs (the test, fluconazole, an episode of cryptococcosis, and the difference in cost between transplant and dialysis), which corresponds most closely to a health care sector perspective. The perspective is not formally stated.
Time horizon. The model has no explicit time dimension. Each input is meant to cover the whole period over which its consequences occur, but the period is not stated, and different inputs may implicitly refer to different periods.
Discounting. No discounting is applied in the model itself. Any discounting would have to be built into the inputs.
Price year. The price year of the costs is not stated.

title: The decision model
text:
Known limitations
The structure above is a simplification. Several of these points are discussed in the evidence review, which also grades the evidence for each input:

A declined kidney is treated as no transplant at all. When a transplant is cancelled after a positive screen, the intended recipient gets the reference outcome (dialysis, zero QALYs gained). In practice most candidates remain on the waiting list and many are transplanted later. The model therefore treats each cancellation as losing the full value of a transplant, q_nocryptococcus, which is likely to overstate the harm of a false-positive screen.
One recipient per donor. A deceased donor usually provides two kidneys to two recipients who share the donor’s infection status and test result. The model follows one donor and one recipient.
Prophylaxis and background disease. After a false-positive screen, prophylaxis is credited with preventing background cryptococcosis over the whole period the input p_spont_cryptococcus covers. Background cryptococcosis often occurs late after transplant, after a short course of prophylaxis would have ended.
No confirmatory testing. A positive screen leads directly to the cancellation and prophylaxis decisions; a second test to confirm or refute it is not modeled.
Single values for disease. Cryptococcosis has one cost and one QALY loss, rather than separate pathways for survival, graft loss and death.
Inputs varied independently. The probabilistic sensitivity analysis draws each uncertain input separately, although some are likely to be related, and holds four inputs fixed. How the inputs are chosen explains the consequences.

Cost effectiveness plane

title: Probabilistic sensitivity analyses
text:
Cost effectiveness acceptability curve
A cost effectiveness acceptability curve estimates the probability of screening being cost-effective as a function of the willingness-to-pay per QALY:

In this case, the probability that screening is cost-effective is 13.6% at $50,000 per QALY and 8.6% at $100,000. It is below 10% for every threshold above about $79,000 per QALY.

title: Probabilistic sensitivity analyses
text:
Summary table
We summarize our findings with the following summary table:

It is not unusual that the mean values from the PSA do not exactly correspond to the base-case results, since the outputs of the model are non-linear in their parameters.
The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected loss, in net monetary benefit, from choosing the wrong strategy given the current uncertainty in the inputs: $3.56 per potential donor, or about $3,557 per 1,000 potential donors. It is an upper limit on what research to remove that uncertainty could be worth for this decision. Whether that is large or small depends on how many donors the decision affects over the years it applies, which the model does not estimate. EVPI reflects only the uncertainty in the inputs, not the structural uncertainty in the model.

title: One-way sensitivity analyses (tornado diagrams)
text:
Tornado diagrams

Tornado diagram for costs

We see that costs are most sensitive to assumptions regarding the cost of an episode of cryptococcal disease post-transplant, cost_disease, and the probability that a donor has cryptococcus, p_donor_cryptococcus.
The expected cost savings from screening, as predicted, increase (become more negative) if those parameters lie at the higher end of the 95% interval.


Tornado diagram for QALYs

We see that QALYs are most sensitive to assumptions regarding the specificity of cryptococcal screening, p_specificity, because each false-positive screen in a donor without cryptococcus can lead to a cancelled transplant.
As predicted, higher values of specificity will lead to less QALY loss from screening. Probability of donor cryptococcus, p_donor_cryptococcus has surprisingly little effect on QALYs.
The QALY gain from a transplant, q_nocryptococcus, is the second-largest driver of QALYs. Its range, from 1.5 to 12.1 QALYs, comes from the shared gamma shape parameter rather than from evidence, and its upper end is likely to be implausibly high for the gain from a single transplant; the evidence review discusses plausible values.

Load the helper functions

source("R/functions.R")

title: Sensitivity analyses
text:
Prior distributions
The list PSA_parameters holds one table each for probabilities, costs and QALYs. Probabilities have Beta priors with \(\alpha\) from shape_parameter and \(\beta = \alpha(1 - \mu)/\mu\). Costs and QALYs have gamma priors with shape \(k\) from shape_parameter and scale \(\theta = \mu/k\). Each table also holds the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, which set the range of the one-way sensitivity analysis. Parameters whose shape is NA are fixed at their base-case value. The base-case values and shape parameters are set on the setup page.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Next, we parameterize the sensitivity analyses.  

#We start with probabilities.  we derive the mean and a shape parameter from the setup file 
#From the mean and alpha, we derive beta and then calculate confidence intervals
PSA_parameters<-list()
PSA_parameters$probabilities<-tribble(
  ~parameter, ~mean, ~shape1,
  "p_usage", expected_value$p_usage, shape_parameter$p_usage,
  "p_donor_cryptococcus",expected_value$p_donor_cryptococcus, shape_parameter$p_donor_cryptococcus, 
  "p_transmission",expected_value$p_transmission,  shape_parameter$p_transmission,
  "p_spont_cryptococcus",expected_value$p_spont_cryptococcus, shape_parameter$p_spont_cryptococcus, 
  "p_sensitivity",expected_value$p_sensitivity, shape_parameter$p_sensitivity,
  "p_specificity",expected_value$p_specificity, shape_parameter$p_specificity,
  "p_cancelled",expected_value$p_cancelled, shape_parameter$p_cancelled,
  "p_prophrate",expected_value$p_prophrate, shape_parameter$p_prophrate,
  "p_prophefficacy",expected_value$p_prophefficacy, shape_parameter$p_prophefficacy)%>%
  mutate(shape2=shape1 * (1 - mean) / mean)%>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(mu=mean(rbeta(1e6, shape1, shape2)), lb_95=qbeta(0.025, shape1, shape2), ub_95=qbeta(0.975, shape1, shape2))
#For costs and QALYS, we start from the mean and shape parameter, and we derive scale and then calculate confidence intervals
PSA_parameters$costs<-tribble(

title: Sensitivity analyses
text:
Probabilistic sensitivity analysis
Each parameter is drawn nsim times from its prior. The derived probabilities are computed for each draw, and calculate_cost_QALY_QC() gives the expected cost and QALYs of each strategy. The incremental cost, QALYs and net monetary benefit of screening are computed for every draw, and a 95% ellipse is fitted to the incremental costs and QALYs. The cost-effectiveness plane is saved as figures/PSA_plot.svg.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Probabilistic sensitivity analysis
#Now, we simulate 10,000 draws from the above.  First, we create the dataset with the simulated values

#Extract values from above
PSA_simulation<-list()
PSA_simulation$probabilities <- PSA_parameters$probabilities %>%
  transmute(
    draws = purrr::map2(shape1, shape2, ~ rbeta(nsim, .x, .y))
  ) %>%
  pull(draws) %>%
  rlang::set_names(PSA_parameters$probabilities$parameter) %>%
  as_tibble()
PSA_simulation$costs<-PSA_parameters$costs %>%
  transmute(
    draws = purrr::map2(shape, scale, ~ rgamma(nsim, shape=.x, scale=.y))
  ) %>%
  pull(draws) %>%
  rlang::set_names(PSA_parameters$costs$parameter) %>%
  as_tibble()%>%
  mutate(cost_cancellation=expected_value$cost_cancellation,
         cost_nocryptococcus=expected_value$cost_nocryptococcus,
         cost_nonacceptance=expected_value$cost_nonacceptance)
PSA_simulation$qalys<-PSA_parameters$qalys %>%
  transmute(
    draws = purrr::map2(shape, scale, ~ rgamma(nsim, shape=.x, scale=.y))
  ) %>%
  pull(draws) %>%
  rlang::set_names(PSA_parameters$qalys$parameter) %>%
  as_tibble()%>%
  mutate(q_noacceptance=expected_value$q_noacceptance)

#Combine into a single tibble
PSA_simulation<-bind_cols(PSA_simulation)%>%
  
  #Add derived quantities
  mutate(
  p_nonusage=1-p_usage,
  p_donor_nocryptococcus=1-p_donor_cryptococcus,
  p_nontransmission=1-p_transmission,
  p_nospont_cryptococcus=1-p_spont_cryptococcus,
  p_falsenegative=1-p_sensitivity,
  p_falsepositive=1-p_specificity,
  p_nocancelled=1-p_cancelled,
  p_noprophrate=1-p_prophrate,
  p_noprophefficacy=1-p_prophefficacy,
  p_breakthrough_donorpos=(1-p_prophefficacy)*p_transmission,
  p_nobreakthrough_donorpos=1-p_breakthrough_donorpos,
  p_breakthrough_donorneg=(1-p_prophefficacy)*p_spont_cryptococcus,
  p_nobreakthrough_donorneg=1-p_breakthrough_donorneg,
  q_cryptococcus=q_nocryptococcus-q_loss_cryptococcus)%>%
  
  #Calculate costs and QALYs
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(results=list(calculate_cost_QALY_QC(p_usage=p_usage, 
                                        p_donor_cryptococcus=p_donor_cryptococcus, 
                                        p_transmission=p_transmission,
                                        p_spont_cryptococcus=p_spont_cryptococcus,
                                        p_sensitivity=p_sensitivity,
                                        p_specificity=p_specificity,
                                        p_cancelled=p_cancelled,
                                        p_prophrate=p_prophrate,
                                        p_prophefficacy=p_prophefficacy,
                                        cost_test=cost_test,
                                        cost_disease=cost_disease,
                                        cost_fluconazole=cost_fluconazole,
                                        cost_cancellation=cost_cancellation,
                                        cost_nocryptococcus=cost_nocryptococcus,
                                        cost_nonacceptance=cost_nonacceptance,
                                        q_nocryptococcus=q_nocryptococcus,
                                        q_noacceptance=q_noacceptance,
                                        q_loss_cryptococcus=q_loss_cryptococcus
  )))%>%
  ungroup()

PSA_simulation_unnested<-PSA_simulation%>%
  unnest(results)%>%
  mutate(cost_change=total_expected_cost_s-total_expected_cost_ns,
         qaly_change=total_expected_qaly_s-total_expected_qaly_ns)%>%
  mutate(icer=cost_change/qaly_change)%>%
  mutate(
    nmb = wtp * qaly_change - cost_change,
    sim_number=row_number()
  )

#Calculate the 95% ellipse
PSA_min_df <- PSA_simulation_unnested %>%
  select(qaly_change, cost_change)

# Create mu and sigma vectors for ellipse
ellipse_mu <- colMeans(PSA_min_df)
ellipse_Sigma <- cov(PSA_min_df)
# Generate ellipse points
ellipse_df <- as.data.frame(
  ellipse(
    ellipse_Sigma,
    centre = ellipse_mu,
    level = 0.95,
    npoints = 200
  )
)
colnames(ellipse_df) <- c("qaly_change", "cost_change")


#Create PSA plot
PSA_plot<-PSA_simulation_unnested%>%
  ggplot()+
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x=qaly_change, y=cost_change), alpha=0.1)+
  geom_path(
    data = ellipse_df,
    color = "red",
    mapping = aes(x=qaly_change, y=cost_change),
    linewidth = 1
  )+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, color = "black")+
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, color = "black")+
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.5, 1.5),
                  ylim = c(-300, 300))+
  theme_classic()+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Probabilistic sensitivity analysis",
    x="QALY change",
    y="Cost change"
  )
ggsave("figures/PSA_plot.svg")
PSA_plot

title: Sensitivity analyses
text:
Acceptability curve, EVPI and BCEA
The acceptability curve gives the share of draws in which screening has positive net monetary benefit at each willingness-to-pay value from $0 to $200,000 per QALY, and is saved as figures/PSA_CEAC_plot.svg. The expected value of perfect information is computed at the willingness-to-pay threshold. A summary table is saved as figures/PSA_summary_table.png and tables/PSA_summary_table.docx. The same draws are then passed to the BCEA package.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Create a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve
#Create a data set that depicts the fraction of simulations that are cost-effective
lambda_grid <- seq(0, 200000, by = 1000)

ceac_df <- expand.grid(
  sim_number = PSA_simulation_unnested$sim_number,
  lambda = lambda_grid
) %>%
  left_join(PSA_simulation_unnested, by = "sim_number") %>%
  mutate(
    nmb = lambda * qaly_change - cost_change
  ) %>%
  group_by(lambda) %>%
  summarise(
    p_ce = mean(nmb > 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#Plot the curve
ggplot(ceac_df, aes(lambda, p_ce)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Willingness-to-pay per QALY",
    y = "Probability cost-effective",
    title = "Cost effectiveness acceptability curve"
  ) +
  theme_classic()+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
ggsave("figures/PSA_CEAC_plot.svg")

#Calculate EVPI
evpi_at_wtp<-with(PSA_simulation_unnested, {
  mean(pmax(nmb, 0)) - pmax(mean(nmb), 0)
})

#We summarize the PSA results in a data frame.
#Note, since the simulation is non-linear, the mean of the simulations wouldn't be expected to exactly be the base case results
PSA_summary_df <- PSA_simulation_unnested %>%
  summarise(
    mean_delta_cost = mean(cost_change),
    mean_delta_qaly = mean(qaly_change),
    mean_nmb        = mean(nmb),
    p_ce            = mean(nmb > 0)
  )%>%
  mutate(evpi=evpi_at_wtp)

PSA_summary_gt<-PSA_summary_df%>%
  gt()%>%
  cols_label(
    mean_delta_cost = "Mean cost change",
    mean_delta_qaly = "Mean QALY change",
    mean_nmb = "Mean NMB",
    p_ce = "Probability of cost effectiveness",
    evpi = "Estimated value of perfect information"
  )%>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(align = "center"),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  )
PSA_summary_gt
PSA_summary_gt%>%
  gtsave("figures/PSA_summary_table.png")
if (file.exists("tables/PSA_summary_table.docx")) {
  unlink("tables/PSA_summary_table.docx")
}
PSA_summary_gt%>%
  gtsave("tables/PSA_summary_table.docx")

#Save the PSA results for the website
write_csv(PSA_summary_df, "output/psa_summary.csv")
write_csv(ceac_df, "output/psa_ceac.csv")
PSA_simulation_unnested%>%
  select(sim_number, cost_change, qaly_change, nmb)%>%
  write_csv("output/psa_draws.csv")

#Now we use the BCEA package in R for further analysis of the PSA data.  We start by creating the matrices needed for the analysis and then creating the BCEA object
PSA_cost_matrix<-PSA_simulation_unnested%>%
  select(starts_with("total_expected_cost"))%>%
  rename(ns=total_expected_cost_ns, s=total_expected_cost_s)%>%
  as.matrix()

PSA_qaly_matrix<-PSA_simulation_unnested%>%
  select(starts_with("total_expected_qaly"))%>%
  rename(ns=total_expected_qaly_ns, s=total_expected_qaly_s)%>%
  as.matrix()

bcea_object<-bcea(eff = PSA_qaly_matrix, cost = PSA_cost_matrix, ref = 2, Kmax = wtp)

#Now we create the plots defined in the BCEA package
ceplane.plot(bcea_object, wtp = wtp, comparison=1)
eib.plot(bcea_object)
contour(bcea_object)
contour2(bcea_object)
ceac.plot(bcea_object)
evi.plot(bcea_object)

#Summary statistics
summary(bcea_object)

title: Sensitivity analyses explained
text: A model’s base case uses one best estimate for every input. Sensitivity analyses ask how much the answer would change if those estimates are wrong. This page explains the four kinds used on this site and how to read their figures. The inputs and their ranges are described on How the inputs are chosen.

title: Sensitivity analyses explained
text:
Kinds of uncertainty
Guidance on modeling practice distinguishes several sources of uncertainty (Briggs et al. 2012):

Parameter uncertainty: the true value of an input, such as the specificity of the CrAg test, is not known exactly. The one-way and probabilistic analyses below address this.
Structural uncertainty: the model itself may be built the wrong way, for example by treating a declined kidney as no transplant at all. Changing input values cannot fix this; it needs a different model, or scenarios that approximate one. The decision model page lists the main structural assumptions.
Heterogeneity: real donors and recipients differ. The model describes an average donor, so its results do not apply equally to, say, a donor with suspected central nervous system infection.

Scenario analyses
A scenario analysis changes one or more inputs to values chosen to answer a specific question, such as “what if a positive screen almost never led to cancellation?”, and reruns the model. Scenarios are useful for inputs that are policy choices rather than uncertain facts, and for exploring combinations of changes. The scenario results show four.

section: One-way sensitivity analysis and tornado diagrams
text:
One-way sensitivity analysis and tornado diagrams
A tornado diagram is a graphical summary of a one-way sensitivity analysis, which examines how sensitive the results of a cost-effectiveness model are to changes in individual input parameters.
In a one-way sensitivity analysis, one parameter is varied at a time across a plausible range (for example, its 95% confidence interval), while all other parameters are held constant at their base-case values. The effect of this variation on the outcome of interest—such as costs or QALYs, is then calculated.
Each horizontal bar in a tornado diagram represents a single model parameter. The length of the bar shows how much the outcome changes when that parameter is varied across its specified range.

Longer bars indicate parameters that have a greater influence on the model results

Shorter bars indicate parameters with relatively little impact

Parameters are ordered from top to bottom by their impact, creating the characteristic “tornado” shape

The center line represents the base-case estimate. Each bar runs from the result at the parameter’s low value to the result at its high value, and colour shows which end is which. For some parameters a higher value lowers the result, so the low end of the bar can sit on the right.
In this model the range for each input is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of its prior distribution, and the model is run three times per input: at the low value, the base-case value and the high value. The figure legend calls these the lower and upper bounds of the “CI”; they are this percentile range, not a confidence interval from data. Inputs that are fixed in the model appear with a bar of zero length.
Two cautions when reading a tornado diagram:

Each bar varies one input alone. If two inputs are uncertain together, their combined effect can be larger than either bar suggests. The probabilistic analysis below varies everything at once.
Bar length reflects the range chosen, not only the input’s importance. An input given a wide range can look influential partly because its range is wide. Here every probability uses the same Beta shape parameter and every cost and QALY the same gamma shape, so the ranges are not tailored to the evidence for each input, as explained on How the inputs are chosen.

The tornado diagrams for this model are on the one-way sensitivity results page.

title: Sensitivity analyses explained
text:
Probabilistic sensitivity analysis
The decision tree analysis in the base case analysis assumes that the parameters of the model are known with certainty.
In reality, the true values of these parameters are unknown. We are either estimating them from prior literature or assuming values based on expert opinion.
A probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) is a way of explicitly ascertaining the effects of that uncertainty on a cost-effectiveness model.
Instead of assigning a single fixed value to each model input (for example, “the probability of cryptococcal transmission is X%”), PSA allows each uncertain parameter to vary across a plausible range based on the available evidence. For each parameter, we specify a prior probability distribution that reflects how uncertain we are about its true value.
The cost effectiveness model is then run many times. In each run, the model randomly draws one value for each parameter from its corresponding distribution and calculates the resulting costs and health outcomes. This produces a distribution of possible results rather than a single point estimate.
For the purposes of this analysis, we have run the analysis 10,000 times.
We can plot the costs and QALYs from each simulation on a two-dimensional plot, yielding a cost-effectiveness plane. From this, we derive a 95% uncertainty ellipse1 representing the joint uncertainty of the true cost and QALY change from screening.

Reading the cost-effectiveness plane
Each point on the cost-effectiveness plane is one simulation: the ΔQ and ΔC of screening for one set of drawn inputs. The cloud of 10,000 points shows the joint uncertainty in cost and health. The site draws an ellipse expected to contain 95% of the points, fitted from the means, spreads and correlation of ΔQ and ΔC (Hout et al. 1994). The ellipse assumes the cloud is roughly oval. If the cloud is skewed or has a long tail, as cost results often do, the ellipse can describe it poorly, and the cloud itself is the better guide.
What matters for the decision is not where the ellipse sits relative to the axes, but how much of the cloud lies below a line through the origin whose slope is the willingness-to-pay threshold, where net monetary benefit is positive. The plane on the results page does not draw that line, so the acceptability curve below is the easier way to read this.


The cost-effectiveness acceptability curve
The cost-effectiveness acceptability curve answers that question for every threshold at once (Hout et al. 1994; Fenwick et al. 2001). For each willingness-to-pay value from $0 to $200,000 per QALY, it plots the proportion of simulations in which screening has positive net monetary benefit. That proportion is read as the probability that screening is cost-effective at that threshold, given the uncertainty described by the prior distributions.

A curve near 1 means screening is cost-effective in almost every simulation at that threshold.
A curve near 0 means it almost never is.
A curve near 0.5 means the evidence is finely balanced, and the decision is uncertain.

The curve says how confident one can be in the decision. It does not say how much is at stake if the decision is wrong. That is what the next measure adds.


The expected value of perfect information
If all uncertainty about the inputs could be removed, decision-makers would always pick the better strategy for the true input values. The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the average gain in net monetary benefit from being able to do so (Wilson 2015; Briggs et al. 2012). In this model it is calculated per donor at the willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000 per QALY: the average, across simulations, of the net monetary benefit of the better strategy in each simulation, minus the net monetary benefit of the strategy that is better on average.
EVPI is an upper limit on what further research could be worth for this decision. It is near zero when the same strategy wins in almost every simulation, however wide the uncertainty, and largest when the decision is finely balanced and a wrong choice is costly. The figure on this site is per donor. The value of research to a health system would be that figure multiplied by the number of donors affected over the period in which the decision applies, which the model does not calculate.


Limits of the probabilistic analysis
The probabilistic analysis only reflects the uncertainty that is put into it. It does not capture structural uncertainty, its ranges are set by shared shape parameters rather than by the evidence for each input, and it draws related inputs independently. Its results are best read alongside the known limitations of the model.
